summary: Weekly POC sync focused on quality regressions observed after prompt tuning. Redwood and Cobalt reviewed evaluation metrics, discussed guardrail strategies (instruction layers + post-filters), and agreed on a regression test plan. Security and data residency questions surfaced and Redwood will provide SOC2/KMS docs. Next steps: Redwood to run regression eval, Cobalt to deliver edge-case prompts, follow-up next week.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for 45 minutes - quick check-in on the quality eval from last week's tuning.
[00:12] Aisha Rahman: Hey Maya, yeah we saw a bump in precision on the core prompts but also new failures on edge cases, some hallucinations.
[00:22] Liam Patel: Quick context: we applied the instruction-layer tweak and a safety post-filter. Primary metric is weighted accuracy, plus a human-rated helpfulness score. On the 1k test set accuracy went from 86 to 90 but the 200-edge set dropped - about 12 regressions.
[00:39] Tom Edwards: The regressions are the pain - some of them are actually business-critical (compliance phrasing). We need to avoid risky outputs.
[00:48] Priya Anand: Example - prompt about account closure, model gave ambiguous next steps that could be interpreted as advising policy not allowed. It's subtle.
[00:58] Maya Chen: Right, that's the tradeoff we talked about - stronger instruction layer can tighten answers but may also over-constrain leading to omissions. We want to tune guardrails instead of bluntly suppressing.
[01:12] Diego Marquez: From security side, we also need to confirm logs, retention and KMS. If we move to Dedicated we'll need customer-managed keys.
[01:22] Liam Patel: For KMS we support both cloud KMS and bring-your-own HSM options; we'll send the integration doc. For now, E2E encryption on rest, and audit logs are available via the Console.
[01:35] Aisha Rahman: On scoring - how are we computing the regression flag? It seemed noisy.
[01:40] Liam Patel: We're using an automated scorer: token-level overlap + a semantic similarity threshold (embedding cosine), then flagged if below threshold or flagged by safety classifier. We also sample for human evaluation - the weekly sample is 200. The regression rate is percent of prompts where automated + human disagree.
[02:05] Tom Edwards: Can we get a breakdown by failure mode? Safety false positive vs omission vs hallucination?
[02:12] Liam Patel: Yes, we categorized the 12 regressions: 5 omissions (model became too terse), 4 hallucinations (new fabrication path), 3 safety false positives (overly cautious).
[02:20] Priya Anand: The hallucinations worry me - the model invented a vendor contact in one case.
[02:25] Maya Chen: That's classic prompt leakage from the training data + new decoding config - we can adjust sampling/penalty and add a guardrail rule to ban named-entity invention, plus add a fallback template: "I don't have that info" with suggested next steps.
[02:38] Diego Marquez: We'll want an audit trail of when those guardrails fire. Also, if you're rewriting outputs we need TTL on cached responses for privacy.
[02:48] Liam Patel: Good note - we have prefix/KV caching controls and TTL per route, we can set short TTL for sensitive routes.
[02:55] Aisha Rahman: On the technical eval, could you run the regression across the 500 prompt set we gave last month? The 200 weekly sampler doesn't cover everything.
[03:03] Liam Patel: Yes - we can run a full regression on the 500 set and provide the CSV of metrics (accuracy, BLEU-ish overlap, embedding similarity, safety flag). We'll also run A/B between prior prompt and tuned prompt.
[03:15] Tom Edwards: How much time will that take?
[03:18] Liam Patel: End-to-end about 24-36 hours for thorough human sampling; automated run is a couple hours. We'll prioritize automated and surface the obvious diffs, then follow up with human review.
[03:28] Maya Chen: For the guardrails approach, we suggested a three-layer approach: 1) Instruction adjustments, 2) deterministic post-filter (regex + named-entity blocklist + policy classifier), 3) fallback templating and soft-fail routing to a conservative model.
[03:46] Priya Anand: Soft-fail routing - you mean fallback to a smaller model or canned response?
[03:50] Maya Chen: Could be either - smaller conservative model or a canned "needs human review" template. We can configure routing policies per route.
[03:58] Diego Marquez: For compliance we need SSO integration notes, RBAC, and long-term audit exports. Also, can we pin models for audit reproducibility?
[04:08] Noah Rivera: Absolutely - you can pin model versions, and the Console keeps per-request model version info and a trace ID for repro. Audit exports can be offloaded to your S3/GCS.
[04:18] Aisha Rahman: One run we did on Vertex had similar regression patterns - curious if this is model-specific or config-specific.
[04:24] Liam Patel: Good question - often it's config + decoding + prompt interplay. We can replicate with same decode hyperparams across model variants. We'll include a comparison vs Anthropic/OpenAI baselines in the report if helpful.
[04:36] Tom Edwards: Cost question - if we add deterministic post-filtering and more human review, costs go up. What are the levers?
[04:43] Maya Chen: Levers: batching, prefix caching, quantized model variants for cheaper inference, and routing by cost tier. Also reduce human sampling frequency once automated metrics stabilize.
[04:55] Priya Anand: For latency SLOs we can't exceed 400ms p95 on customer-facing flows. Some of the tuned configs increased latency.
[05:02] Liam Patel: That's where batching vs dedicated capacity tradeoffs matter. If latency is critical we recommend Dedicated or reserved capacity with optimized kernels. We'll run a dedicated benchmark in APAC like you asked.
[05:12] Aisha Rahman: One more practical ask: can you include the prompt before/after in the report so we can audit changes?
[05:18] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll include a diff view of prompt versions and the exact instruction layer edits plus the post-filter rules.
[05:25] Tom Edwards: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[05:28] Maya Chen: Recap - Redwood runs regression on 500 prompts, share CSV and human-sampled failure breakdown, send SOC2/KMS docs, we'll add guardrail rules for named-entity invention and set TTL on caches for those routes, customer to upload 200 edge-case prompts, schedule follow-up next Tuesday same time.
[05:45] Diego Marquez: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[05:48] Aisha Rahman: Thanks, appreciate it.
[05:50] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. Bye.
